[MUQATIL:16:14-17/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Creator of all the preceding things is unlike idols such as al-Lat, al-Uzza, Manat, and Hubal, which create nothing; people should reflect and affirm God's oneness.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p55#2/r6] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | In the question about who creates, the intended creator is God Himself.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p56/r1] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The non-creators are idols; God and the idols worshipped besides Him are unequal because idols control neither harm, benefit, death, life, nor resurrection.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p56/r2] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Al-nushūr means resurrection.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p56/r3] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The address is to the polytheists; the believers are the ones who take heed.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p56/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says God is the Creator, while the idols worshipped besides Him create nothing.
[FARRA:v2p97/r7] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | من may refer to a nonhuman in أفمن يخلق because the created entity is paired with the Creator; the phrase about animals also uses من, and Arabic uses it for a rider and his mount when treated together. | mentions 24:45
[THALABI:v6p12/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The creator, God, cannot be compared with idols that create nothing; the comparison calls people to remember. | mentions 31:11, 46:4
[THALABI:v6p12/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | He links the argument to the verses challenging people to show what other gods created. | mentions 31:11, 46:4
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the creator is God and those who do not create are the idols mentioned in this surah, as in the statement this is God's creation. | mentions 31:11
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra explains the use of man for idols by their association in the sentence with the Creator; Arabs similarly pair a human rider with his camel under man. | mentions 24:45
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | Another view says the idols are addressed as man because people worshiped them, just as a verse asks whether idols have feet. | mentions 7:195
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the question addresses the polytheists: will they not take heed as the believers did?
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أصحابنا | holds | Al-Wahidi's associates argue that the verse establishes one Creator, distinguished from creatures by the power to originate creation; one who claims to create his own acts makes himself God's partner in creation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p37/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل التأويل | reports | Exegetes say the verse denies that creator and noncreator can be treated equally in worship, just as one should not give equal thanks to a benefactor and a non-benefactor.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:17/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The creator is God, mentioned earlier in the surah; the noncreator is the idols.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:17/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The question asks whether creator and noncreator are equal and deserve equal worship; it calls people to take heed.
[JISHUMI:v6p4011/r18] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | God, who creates, is not equal in worship to idols, which create nothing and neither benefit nor harm; the question calls people to reflect.
[JISHUMI:v6p4011/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Although idols are inanimate, the verse uses the rational relative form because it speaks of creation, an act of rational agents, or because worshippers treat idols as rational.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p14/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The one who creates is God; the one who does not create is the idols.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p14/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The question calls people to recognize the difference between God and idols.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p385/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The verse confronts them with the distinction between the one who creates and originates things and those unable to do any such thing.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p385/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The challenge continues by rebuking them with ‘will you not reflect?’
[TABRISI:16:17-18/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The verse asks whether the creator of all things deserves worship like idols that create nothing; equating them is manifest error.
[TABRISI:16:17-18/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Man is used of non-rational things because the clause follows mention of creating.
[TABRISI:16:17-18/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The address urges idolaters to reflect and recognize their flagrant error.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p283/r9] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | A Qur'anic sense of خلق is forming or shaping, as in forming from clay and the contrast between idols and their makers.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p437/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The one who does not create refers to idols; the polytheists treated them as if they had reason and discernment.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p437/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The address challenges the polytheists to take heed as the believers did.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p437/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farraʾ explains that man is grammatically possible for the non-creator because it is paired with the creator, just as it can cover a human and an animal when they are mentioned together. | mentions 24:45
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although an objector expects the comparison to be reversed, the wording stresses how impossible it is to equate the maker of immense benefits with contemptible, inert things in naming, worship, and reverence.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض أصحابنا | reports | Some of al-Rāzī's associates infer that servants do not create their own acts: if creating anything made a being divine, humans who create acts would also have to be gods, which is false.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites answer that the verse contrasts the Creator of the heavens, earth, humans, animals, plants, seas, stars, and mountains with beings unable to create anything; this does not address a servant's acts.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites also say the verse establishes that a creator is superior to a non-creator and should not be equated with one in worship, but it does not make every creator a god. | mentions 7:195
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | Their analogy is that a person with working legs is better than an idol unable to walk and should not worship the inferior idol; this does not make the person a god, just as creating alone does not imply divinity. | mentions 7:195
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After presenting the ordered signs as proofs of a wise Creator and explanations of His blessings, the passage rejects worship of anything besides Him, especially inert objects.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Creator of the listed things cannot be equated with beings unable to create anything; even basic awareness shows worship belongs only to the greatest benefactor, never to lifeless idols without understanding, power, or choice.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The non-creators are idols: inert beings, although min normally marks rational beings.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One answer to using rational min for idols is that unbelievers called them gods and worshipped them, so they are grammatically treated like rational beings. | mentions 16:20
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second explanation for min is stylistic matching with the preceding min in the phrase about the Creator.
[RAZI-FULL:v20p11/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third answer means the Creator is unlike even non-creating rational beings, much more unlike idols; the question about idols' limbs shows their inferiority to living people, not that such limbs would make them worthy of worship. | mentions 7:195
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The one who creates is God, while those who do not create are the idols.
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Idols neither create nor harm nor benefit; the creator is more entitled to worship than created things that cannot help or harm.
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The idols are referred to with the personal interrogative من because Arabs speak of them as persons when worshipping them; compare the question about their limbs in 7:195. | mentions 7:195
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another explanation for من is its proximity to the pronoun associated with the Creator.
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ compares this usage to asking which is which when a rider and his camel are confused, although one is not human.
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī says من may ask about the Creator, but ما asks about kinds, and God is not a member of a kind; Moses answered Pharaoh’s من-question but turned aside from the malformed ما-question. | mentions 20:49, 26:23
[QURTUBI-FULL:16:17/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The creation argument is supported by the challenge to show what anyone besides God has created in 31:11 and 35:40. | mentions 31:11, 35:40
[BAYDAWI-FULL:16:17/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The question denies equivalence after proofs of God’s power, wisdom, and exclusive creation; one unable to create cannot share His divinity.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:16:17/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685

 · author | holds | The expected comparison would ask whether the non-creator equals the Creator; reversing it highlights that idolatry makes God seem like powerless created beings.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:16:17/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Those who do not create include every being worshipped besides God, rational beings or idols; they are treated as rational because called gods, or for stylistic matching and emphasis.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:16:17/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They should recognize the error because it is so evident that slight recollection and attention suffice.

[NASAFI-FULL:v2p252#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Man, normally for rational beings, is used because the idolaters named and worshipped idols as gods; alternatively, the comparison first means one rational creator is unlike a rational noncreator, much less an unintelligent object.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p252#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The wording reverses the surface expectation to refute idolaters who equate idols with God: by making idols God's equals, they make God like created things, so the verse denies that a creator resembles a noncreator.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p252#3/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The verse is an argument against the Muʿtazila concerning the creation of acts.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p252#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The closing question urges them to recognize the error of their position.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari asks why the argument does not reverse the comparison, then answers that idolaters made God resemble creatures by equating them in naming and worship.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The rebuke أفلا تذكرون says this distinction should not be overlooked.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Creator is unlike idols and other worshiped beings that create nothing, so worship belongs to the one who originates creation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The second من may include rational and irrational objects of worship, reflect the pagans' belief in idols' effects, parallel من يخلق, or restrict the comparison to beings with understanding.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | If this means all things worshipped besides God, من is apt because rational beings dominate the mixed class; ما would also be permissible.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | For idols, من may treat them as rational beings because worshippers regard them as able to harm and benefit; the bird-flock poem also uses من for birds.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second explanation for applying من to idols is syntactic correspondence with the preceding من يخلق.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third explanation reserves من for rational beings: if rational non-creators are unworthy of worship, lifeless idols are still less worthy; the cited challenge is 7:195. | mentions 7, :, 1, 9, 5
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قطرب | reports | On Qutrub's view that من may refer to non-rational things under a condition, its use here needs no further explanation.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari asks why the wording does not instead ask whether a non-creator is like the Creator, if idolaters equate idols with God.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:17/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari answers that by naming and worshipping idols as God, idolaters made them like God and hence like created things; the verse rejects this.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p564/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God's greatness means worship belongs to Him alone, unlike idols that create nothing and are themselves created.
[BURHAN:v3p427/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The reversed question confronts idolaters on their own terms: since they elevate non-creators as gods, it applies the stronger argument by lowering the sacred Creator rather than raising the deficient idols.
[BURHAN:v3p427/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · السكاكي | reports | Al-Sakkākī says ‘who does not create’ means a living, capable creator, indirectly rejecting any comparison between idols and God a fortiori.
[BURHAN:v4p412/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The uncreating referent may be idols, described with the rational relative man because Arabs treated them as objects of worship.
[BURHAN:v4p412/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Alternatively, man covers all beings worshiped besides God, rational and nonrational, using the rational form by predominance in a mixed group. | mentions 24:45
[BURHAN:v4p412/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In an example listing crawling creatures, man applies to snakes and animals because rational and nonrational referents mix, so the rational form predominates. | mentions 24:45
[BURHAN:v4p412/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | One explanation says ma is more common because nonrational things and their grammatical contexts are more numerous; man is reserved for the less common rational cases for stylistic fit.
[BURHAN:v4p412/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · الإبياري | reports | Al-Ibyari says the man/ma distinction applies to relative pronouns only, not conditionals, which require a verb and do not govern nouns.
[BURHAN:v4p412/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The relative man can take a singular verb by form and a plural predicate by meaning, as in the wording about those who are Jews or Christians. | mentions 2:135
[BURHAN:v4p56/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | من is used for idols, although ما is normal for nonrational things, because the audience treats the idols as deities; the author answers that the wording aims to make the intended target clear to them.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Reversing the comparison would lose the force of lowering the higher party to the incapable idols' level and thereby rebuking their worshippers.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Calling the idols 'who' treats them as if they were rational because their worshippers named them gods; if they fail at creation, their divinity is all the more impossible.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The closing question urges reflection on the visible evidence, even from some angles, so people will abandon associating partners with God.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The full arrangement and clarity of the signs leaves no doubt that Allah alone is Creator, given His oneness, knowledge, power, and wisdom, the signs' universal benefit, and idols' incapacity.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Differences in existence and qualities where no cause except choice explains them show that God acts by choice and can bring about whatever He wills.
[BIQAI-FULL:v4p255/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The rhetorical comparison asks whether the One who continually creates as He wills can be like idols, which never create and are therefore contingent and incapable.
[DURR-FULL:v5p119/r2] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · قتادة | reports | Qatada says God is the Creator and Provider, whereas the idols worshipped besides Him create nothing and can neither harm nor benefit their worshippers.
[ITQAN:v3p118/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Although the apparent comparison is reversed, it answers idolaters who made non-creators like the Creator through excessive worship, treating idols as the norm; the response mirrors their distorted ordering.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The creator is God, who makes the wondrous things just listed or whatever He wills; the noncreator makes nothing, great or small. The comparison rebukes idolatry by denying any likeness between God and idols.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The fāʾ after the interrogative hamza directs the denial to the supposed inference of likeness from God's preceding mighty acts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Creation is singled out from the preceding acts because it is their greatest and clearest instance, or because each preceding act is itself a particular creation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Although one might expect the negative comparison first, the chosen order respects possession's precedence over absence and stresses that shirk lowers lordship to the level of inert matter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The noncreator may mean all noncreating beings, intelligent and inanimate, with من favoring rational beings; alternatives are intelligent beings alone with idols inferred a fortiori, or idols alone, but Alusi prefers the broader reading.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Idols fall under the denial either directly or by an a-fortiori inference: if even intelligent noncreators are unlike God, inert idols are still less comparable.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p117/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Alusi notes that the verse is used to refute the Muʿtazilite doctrine that human beings create their own acts.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p123/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The rhetorical question denies any equality between creator and noncreator; the comparison targets the polytheists' treatment of idols as God's partners and shows who merits divinity.

[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The closing verses of the preceding argument summarize its detailed case and infer divine oneness: God alone creates, bestows innumerable blessings, knows the hidden and open, owns all, and governs all.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The integrated proof is directed against polytheists who deny God’s sole lordship, not against people who deny a creator.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعضهم | rejects | Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the claim that the passage establishes tawhid through two independent proofs, creation and blessing: creation alone proves a maker and unity in creating, not exclusive lordship over polytheists.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The polytheists already accepted God as creator of everything, even their idols, while claiming idols received delegated control of the world and intercession; creation alone would not answer that claim.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The creation argument establishes that God alone is the true benefactor: all beings and the benefits arising from them belong to Him as absolute, inalienable ownership.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The rhetorical question denies equality between God and what others invoke; its interrogative form expresses repudiation.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Those who do not create are the deities people invoke apart from God.
[TABATABAI:16:17-19/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God continuously creates things and therefore owns their existence, effects, particular systems, and the universal order; He cannot equal one who creates nothing.
[ASAD-NOTES:16:17/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The creator cannot be equated with beings unable to create, a contrast meant to prompt reflection.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p312/r11] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The verse directs readers to the implications of monotheism and accountability in the Hereafter.
